title: The Invention in the Drawer
subtitle: Kodak built the world's first digital camera in 1975 — and then put it away. Every year after that, waiting looked like the sensible choice.

vocab.def: A new thing that nobody made before. The verb is to invent.
vocab.ex: The digital camera was a Kodak invention.

vocab.def: The special plastic that old cameras used to record pictures. You bought it, used it, then bought more.
vocab.ex: Kodak sold film all over the world.

vocab.def: The money a company keeps after it pays all its costs.
To take the place of something old.
A company or person you compete against.
To do something later than planned.
vocab.ex: Kodak delayed the change for many years.

vocab.def: Reasonable; a good idea when you think about it carefully.
vocab.ex: Every year, waiting looked like the sensible choice.

vocab.def: To close something completely — a factory, a business, a machine.
vocab.ex: Kodak shut down factories and sold divisions.

vocab.def: With no money left to pay what you owe. The noun is bankruptcy.
To continue to exist after something bad happens.

items: The shop made no ___ last year, so the owner closed it.
It isn't ___ to drive when you are so tired.
We had to ___ the meeting because two people were ill.
Email has almost completely ___ the paper letter.
The factory will ___ ___ next year and 400 people will lose their jobs.
Our main ___ opened a bigger shop across the road.

vocab_discuss: Do you have any old photographs printed on paper? Who keeps them?
Think of something that has replaced something else in your life in the last ten years.
Is it always sensible to wait before making a big change? When is it not?

story.heading: Part 1 — "That's cute — but don't tell anyone"
paras: In December 1975, a young engineer called Steven Sasson finished a strange machine. He worked for Kodak, in New York. He was twenty-five years old.
His machine was as big as a toaster. It weighed four kilos. It took twenty-three seconds to record one picture, and the picture was black and white and very small.
It was useless. It was also the first digital camera in the world.
Sasson showed it to the bosses. Their answer became famous. They said: that's nice — but don't tell anybody about it.

They were not stupid. Kodak was one of the most famous companies on earth, and its business was beautiful. Cameras were cheap. Film was not. Every birthday, every holiday, every wedding — people bought film, and then they paid to print the photographs.
Sasson was showing them a future with no film in it.
tf: The first digital camera was invented by a company that competed with Kodak.
The first digital camera took very good colour pictures.
Kodak made most of its money from selling cameras.
discuss: Kodak made cameras cheap but film expensive. Why was that a clever way to make money?
The bosses said "don't tell anybody". Can you understand why? Were they right?

story.heading: Part 2 — The maths trap
paras: Here is the part most people do not know: Kodak did not ignore digital. It kept inventing. It built better sensors. It sold digital cameras in the 1990s. For thirty years, Kodak knew more about digital photography than almost anybody.
The problem was not the technology. The problem was the numbers.
Film made about sixty or seventy cents of profit in every dollar. Electronics made a few cents. So every dollar Kodak earned from digital destroyed several dollars from film.
And there was something worse. The damage to film hurt only Kodak. But the digital market was open to Sony, Canon and everybody else.
One phrase went around the company for years: we are trading high-margin dollars for low-margin pennies.
So every single year, waiting one more year looked sensible. And the people deciding how fast digital should come were the same people whose skills digital would destroy.
Film sales kept growing until about the year 2000. That growth became the argument for staying calm.
tf: Kodak stopped inventing digital technology after 1975.
Film made much more profit than electronics.
Film sales were already falling in the 1990s.
discuss: Explain the "dollars and pennies" problem in your own words.
Every year, waiting was the sensible choice. So when exactly should Kodak have changed?

story.heading: Part 3 — One drowned, one learned to swim
paras: Around 2000 the market turned, and it turned fast. Film sales fell by half. Then by half again.

Kodak cut jobs, shut down factories and sold parts of the company. In January 2012 it went bankrupt. The company that gave photography to ordinary people, and that put the words Kodak moment into a dozen languages, could not pay its bills.
Now here is the part that makes this story so useful. There was another company in exactly the same situation.
Fujifilm was Kodak's oldest rival. Same industry, same product, same problem, same year. But Fujifilm decided something early and hard: film is finished, whatever we do.

So it took the money from the dying film business and put it into anything its chemistry knowledge could reach — medicines, skin care, materials for flat screens. Today Fujifilm is a large healthcare and materials company.
Same wave. One company drowned. One learned to surf.
Kodak said, "we are a film company." Fujifilm said, "we are a chemistry company." That one sentence decided everything.
So the question is not whether a company can see the future. Kodak saw it first, in 1975. The question is who is allowed to say out loud that the old money is already gone.
tf: Fujifilm had a completely different business from Kodak.
Fujifilm decided early that film had no future.
discuss: Fujifilm said "we are a chemistry company", not "a film company". Why did that change everything?
Was Kodak unlucky, or did it make bad decisions? What do you think?
Tell the story in six sentences. Use: invented · because · so · delayed · but · in the end.

grammar.name: because, so, but
grammar.heading: Joining ideas: because, so, but
explain: This story is all about reasons and results. Kodak did something because of the money, so something happened, but the end was bad. These three little words do most of the work when you explain a business decision.
because + a reason. It answers why? → "Kodak waited because film made more profit."
so + a result. It answers what happened next? → "Film made more profit, so Kodak waited."
but + a surprise or a difference. → "Kodak invented the camera, but it did not sell it."
The most useful thing to notice: because and so say the same thing in opposite directions. Learn to turn one into the other and you can say any idea two ways.

practice.heading: Complete the sentences about the story
practice.intro: Write because, so or but in each gap. Read the whole sentence before you choose.
items: Kodak invented the digital camera, ___ it did not want to sell it.
Film was very profitable, ___ every year Kodak waited one more year.
The bosses were worried ___ digital would destroy their best business.
Fujifilm and Kodak had the same problem, ___ only one of them survived.
Fujifilm moved into medicine and cosmetics ___ it understood chemistry.

fix.heading: Say it the other way
fix.intro: Each sentence uses because. Say it again with so — the meaning must stay the same. Then check.
items: Kodak delayed because film made more money.
The bosses said nothing because they were afraid of the future.
Fujifilm survived because it changed early.
Film sales fell because people bought digital cameras.
Kodak went bankrupt because it changed too late.
answers: Film made more money, so Kodak delayed.
The bosses were afraid of the future, so they said nothing.
People bought digital cameras, so film sales fell.
Kodak changed too late, so it went bankrupt.

speak.label: 1 · Tell the story
paras: Tell me the story of Kodak in your own words. Six or seven sentences is enough.

speak.label: 2 · A decision you delayed
paras: Tell me about something you waited too long to do. Why did you wait?
Use because and so at least twice each.

speak.label: 3 · Two companies, one problem
paras: Kodak and Fujifilm had the same problem and did different things.
Tell me the difference between them, and say which one you would have worked for.

speak.label: 4 · Your opinion
paras: Is it possible for a very successful company to change before it has to?
What would have to be true inside the company? Give one example.

final: Do you take photographs? Do you ever print them? Why, or why not?
"We are not a film company, we are a chemistry company." How would you describe your own job in that way?
Which is more dangerous for a company: a bad product, or a very profitable old one?
